claims.text: Adding a small amount of a low-melting sintering aid promotes formation of a transient liquid phase during sintering.
Transient liquid-phase formation reduces the required sintering temperature.
The reduction in sintering temperature results from increased mass transport at particle interfaces.
The initial ceramic powder has a high intrinsic sintering temperature and contains no additives.
A controlled concentration of a low-melting oxide, such as an alkali or alkaline-earth oxide, can be used as a sintering aid.
Transient liquid phases form at particle boundaries during heating.
The low-melting sintering aid melts at a temperature below that required for conventional solid-state sintering.
The resulting liquid phase facilitates particle rearrangement.
The resulting liquid phase enhances diffusion.
Enhanced particle rearrangement and diffusion promote densification below the temperatures required for solid-state sintering.
Doped samples will achieve densification comparable to undoped samples at a lower sintering temperature.
Doped samples will exhibit an earlier onset of densification.
Doped samples will exhibit microstructural evidence of liquid-phase-assisted grain bonding.
Undoped ceramic powder requires higher temperatures to attain full densification.
Excessive sintering-aid concentration may cause abnormal grain growth or phase segregation.
Very low sintering-aid concentrations may be insufficient to induce a transient liquid phase.
The reduction in sintering temperature and optimum additive concentration depend on the ceramic composition and the selected sintering aid.
